title: Coordinate Geometry: Distance, Midpoint and Gradient
summary: The formulas for the distance between two points, the midpoint of a line segment and the gradient, and the point dividing a line in a ratio.

p: Every point has coordinates (x, y), where x is the distance across from the origin and y is the distance up. Let A(x₁, y₁) and B(x₂, y₂) be two points. We use A(1, 2) and B(7, 10) in the examples.
AB = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²). This comes from Pythagoras' theorem. For A(1, 2) and B(7, 10): AB = √(6² + 8²) = √100 = 10.
The midpoint M has coordinates ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2). For A and B: M = ((1 + 7)/2, (2 + 10)/2) = (4, 6).
m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). For A and B: m = 8/6 = 4/3. A vertical line has no gradient (undefined). A horizontal line has gradient 0.

sections.h: Point dividing a line in a ratio
p: The point P that divides AB in the ratio m : n (from A to B) is ((n x₁ + m x₂)/(m + n), (n y₁ + m y₂)/(m + n)). For A(1, 2), B(7, 10) and ratio 1 : 2, P = ((2 × 1 + 1 × 7)/3, (2 × 2 + 1 × 10)/3) = (3, 14/3). The midpoint is the special case m = n.
1. Show that the triangle P(0, 0), Q(3, 4), R(6, 0) is isosceles. PQ = 5, QR = √(9 + 16) = 5 and PR = 6. Two sides are equal, so it is isosceles.
2. The midpoint of AB is (2, 3) and A is (−1, 5). Find B. (−1 + x)/2 = 2 so x = 5; (5 + y)/2 = 3 so y = 1. B = (5, 1).
3. Are (2, 3), (5, 9) and (8, 15) on one line? The gradient from the first to the second is 6/3 = 2, and from the second to the third is 6/3 = 2. Yes: they are collinear.

title: The Equation of a Straight Line
summary: The four forms of a straight-line equation, and the conditions for lines to be parallel or perpendicular.

p: 1. Slope-intercept form: y = mx + c (m = gradient, c = y-intercept).
2. Point-slope form: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).
3. Two-point form: (y − y₁)/(y₂ − y₁) = (x − x₁)/(x₂ − x₁).
4. General form: ax + by + c = 0.
2. Gradient 3 through (2, 7): y − 7 = 3(x − 2), so y = 3x + 1.
3. Find the gradient and intercepts of 3x + 2y = 12: y = −1.5x + 6. m = −1.5; y-intercept 6; x-intercept 4.
Parallel lines have the same gradient: m₁ = m₂. Perpendicular lines have gradients whose product is −1: m₁ m₂ = −1.
Example 1. The line through (5, 8) parallel to y = 2x − 3: gradient 2, so y − 8 = 2(x − 5), giving y = 2x − 2.
Example 2. The line through the origin perpendicular to 4x + 3y = 12. The gradient of 4x + 3y = 12 is −4/3, so the perpendicular has gradient 3/4: y = (3/4)x.
Example 3. Are y = 3x + 2 and y = −x/3 + 5 perpendicular? 3 × (−1/3) = −1, so yes.
Example 4. Show that 2x + 3y = 15 and 3x − 2y = 10 are perpendicular. m₁ = −2/3 and m₂ = 3/2, and the product is −1.
A line with x-intercept a and y-intercept b has the equation x/a + y/b = 1. For intercepts 4 and 6, x/4 + y/6 = 1, which is 3x + 2y = 12.

title: Intersecting Lines, Perpendicular Bisectors and Area of a Triangle
summary: Finding where two lines meet, the perpendicular bisector of a segment, and the area of a triangle from its coordinates.

p: Solve the two equations together. 2x + y = 7 and x − y = 2: add them to get 3x = 9, so x = 3 and y = 1. The lines meet at (3, 1).

The perpendicular bisector of AB passes through the midpoint and is perpendicular to AB. For A(1, 2) and B(7, 10): midpoint (4, 6); gradient of AB = 4/3; gradient of the bisector = −3/4. Then y − 6 = −(3/4)(x − 4), so 4y − 24 = −3x + 12 and 3x + 4y = 36.
Check: the point (0, 9) is on this line, and it is √50 from A and from B.

Find the equation of the set of points P(x, y) that are equidistant from A(1, 2) and B(7, 10). PA² = PB²: (x − 1)² + (y − 2)² = (x − 7)² + (y − 10)². Expanding: −2x − 4y + 5 = −14x − 20y + 149, so 12x + 16y = 144 and 3x + 4y = 36. This is the perpendicular bisector again.
For vertices (x₁, y₁), (x₂, y₂), (x₃, y₃): area = ½ |x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)|.
Example. (1, 1), (5, 1) and (3, 5): ½ |1(1 − 5) + 5(5 − 1) + 3(1 − 1)| = ½ |−4 + 20 + 0| = 8. Check: base 4, height 4, area ½ × 4 × 4 = 8. If the area is 0, the three points are collinear.

title: Locus: The Basic Loci
summary: What a locus is, and the four basic loci: a circle, a perpendicular bisector, an angle bisector and a pair of parallel lines.

p: A locus (plural loci) is the set of all the points that satisfy a given condition or rule. For example, the locus of points that are 4 cm from a fixed point P is a circle of radius 4 cm with centre P.

img.alt: Three diagrams: a circle as the locus of points a fixed distance from a point, a perpendicular bisector as the locus of points equidistant from A and B, and an angle bisector as the locus of points equidistant from two lines

sections.h: 1. Fixed distance from a point: a circle
p: Mark point P. Set a compass to the distance (say 4 cm). Put the point on P and draw a complete circle.

sections.h: 2. Equidistant from two points: the perpendicular bisector
p: Draw AB = 6 cm. Open the compass to more than half of AB (say 4 cm). With centre A draw arcs above and below AB. With centre B and the same radius draw arcs that cross the first ones. Join the two crossing points P and Q. The line PQ is the perpendicular bisector of AB: every point on it is the same distance from A and B.

sections.h: 3. Equidistant from two intersecting lines: the angle bisector
p: Draw angle ABC. With centre B draw an arc that cuts both arms at P and Q. With centres P and Q and the same radius, draw arcs that cross at R. Join B to R. The line BR bisects the angle: every point on it is the same distance from the two arms.

sections.h: 4. Fixed distance from a line: two parallel lines
p: The locus of points 3 cm from a line AB is a pair of parallel lines, one on each side of AB, each 3 cm from it (with semicircles at the ends if the line is a segment).

The locus of points 5 units from the origin is x² + y² = 25. The locus of points equidistant from (0, 0) and (4, 0) is the line x = 2. The locus of points equidistant from the x-axis and the y-axis is the pair of lines y = x and y = −x.

title: Intersection of Loci and Practical Problems
summary: Combining two or more loci to find a required point or region, with worked problems.

p: Often a point must satisfy two conditions at once. We draw both loci. The required points are where they cross. If a region is wanted, we shade the part that satisfies all the conditions.

Points are 5 cm from A and 3 cm from B, where AB = 6 cm. Draw a circle of radius 5 cm at A and a circle of radius 3 cm at B. They cut at two points, P and Q. By calculation with A(0, 0) and B(6, 0): x² + y² = 25 and (x − 6)² + y² = 9. Subtract: −12x + 36 = −16, so x = 4.33. Then y² = 25 − 18.78 = 6.22 and y = ±2.49. The points are (4.33, 2.49) and (4.33, −2.49).

sections.h: Example 2: a perpendicular bisector and a circle
p: Find the points that are equidistant from A and B and also 4 cm from a point C. Draw the perpendicular bisector of AB and a circle of radius 4 cm centred on C. The points where the line cuts the circle are the answers (there may be 0, 1 or 2 of them).

A telephone mast is to be placed so that it is less than 5 km from town A, at least 3 km from town B, and nearer to A than to B. Draw (1) a circle of radius 5 km at A and shade inside it; (2) a circle of radius 3 km at B and shade outside it; (3) the perpendicular bisector of AB and shade the side nearer to A. The region where all three shadings overlap is where the mast can be placed.

A dog is tied by a 6 m rope to one corner of a rectangular shed 4 m long and 3 m wide. Outside the shed it can reach three-quarters of a circle of radius 6 m. When the rope wraps round the corner 4 m away, 2 m of rope is left, giving a quarter circle of radius 2 m. When it wraps round the corner 3 m away, 3 m is left, giving a quarter circle of radius 3 m. Area = (3/4)π(6²) + (1/4)π(2²) + (1/4)π(3²) = π(27 + 1 + 2.25) = 30.25π ≈ 95.0 m².

title: Circumcircle, Incircle and Escribed Circle of a Triangle
summary: The three circles connected with a triangle, how to construct them, and the formulas for their radii.

p: The circumcircle is the circle that passes through all three vertices of a triangle. Its centre, the circumcentre O, is the point where the perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet. Construction: draw triangle ABC; construct the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC; they meet at O; with centre O and radius OA, draw the circle through A, B and C.
For a right-angled triangle, the circumcentre is the midpoint of the hypotenuse.

The incircle touches all three sides from the inside. Its centre, the incentre I, is where the angle bisectors meet. Construction: bisect two of the angles; they meet at I; drop a perpendicular from I to one side to find the radius; draw the circle.

img.alt: A triangle with its circumcircle through the three vertices and the perpendicular bisectors meeting at O, and another triangle with its incircle and angle bisectors meeting at I

p: An escribed circle touches one side of the triangle and the extensions of the other two sides, from outside. Its centre is where the bisector of one interior angle meets the bisectors of the two exterior angles at the other vertices. A triangle has three escribed circles.
Let the sides be a, b, c, the semi-perimeter s = (a + b + c)/2 and the area K. Circumradius R = abc/(4K). Inradius r = K/s. Exradius opposite a: rₐ = K/(s − a).

Example 1. A 3, 4, 5 triangle: K = 6, s = 6. R = (3 × 4 × 5)/(4 × 6) = 2.5, which is half the hypotenuse. r = 6/6 = 1. Exradii: opposite 3: 6/(6 − 3) = 2; opposite 4: 6/(6 − 4) = 3; opposite 5: 6/(6 − 5) = 6.

title: Differentiation: Limits and the Idea of a Derivative
summary: The idea of a limit, the gradient of a curve at a point as a limit of gradients of chords, and the meaning of the derivative.

p: Calculus is the mathematics of change. It has two parts: differentiation, which finds how fast something changes (the gradient of a curve), and integration, which adds up many small quantities (such as areas).

lim (x → a) f(x) = L means that f(x) gets as near as we like to L when x gets near to a. Examples. lim (x → 5) (x² + 2x) = 25 + 10 = 35. lim (x → 4) (x² − 16)/(x − 4): we cannot put x = 4 (we would divide by zero), so first simplify: (x − 4)(x + 4)/(x − 4) = x + 4, and the limit is 8. lim (h → 0) [(3 + h)² − 9]/h = lim (6 + h) = 6. lim (x → 2) (x³ − 8)/(x − 2) = lim (x² + 2x + 4) = 12.

The gradient of a straight line is the same everywhere. The gradient of a curve changes from point to point. The gradient of the curve at a point is the gradient of the tangent to the curve at that point.

To find it, take a second point near P on the curve and find the gradient of the chord joining them. As the second point moves closer to P, the chord gets closer to the tangent. The gradient of the tangent is the limit of the gradients of the chords.

title: Differentiation from First Principles and the Power Rule
summary: The definition of the derivative as a limit, worked from first principles, and the power rule for differentiating xⁿ.

p: dy/dx = lim (h → 0) [f(x + h) − f(x)] / h. This is the gradient of the chord from x to x + h as h tends to 0.
1. f(x) = x². [(x + h)² − x²]/h = (2xh + h²)/h = 2x + h. As h → 0 this gives 2x. So d(x²)/dx = 2x.
2. f(x) = x³. [(x + h)³ − x³]/h = (3x²h + 3xh² + h³)/h = 3x² + 3xh + h². As h → 0: 3x².
3. f(x) = 3x + 2. [3(x + h) + 2 − 3x − 2]/h = 3h/h = 3. The derivative is 3 (the gradient of the line).
4. f(x) = x² + 4x. The derivative is 2x + 4.
If y = xⁿ, then dy/dx = n xⁿ⁻¹. The constant multiple rule: d/dx (c f(x)) = c f′(x). The sum and difference rules: d/dx (f ± g) = f′ ± g′. The derivative of a constant is 0.
Examples. y = x⁵ gives 5x⁴. y = 4x³ gives 12x². y = 3x² + 5x − 2 gives 6x + 5. y = 4x³ − 7x² + 2x − 9 gives 12x² − 14x + 2. y = 5x⁴ − 3x² + 7 gives 20x³ − 6x.

Negative and fractional powers: write the function as powers of x. y = 2/x = 2x⁻¹ gives −2x⁻² = −2/x². y = 3√x = 3x^(1/2) gives (3/2)x^(−1/2) = 3/(2√x). y = (2x² + 3)/x = 2x + 3x⁻¹ gives 2 − 3/x². y = 3√x + 2/x gives 3/(2√x) − 2/x².
Value at a point. f(x) = x⁵: f′(2) = 5 × 2⁴ = 80. y = x³ at x = 1: the gradient is 3 × 1² = 3.

title: Tangents, Normals and the Meaning of the Derivative
summary: Finding the equation of the tangent and the normal to a curve at a point, and interpreting the derivative as a rate of change.

p: Steps: 1. Find dy/dx. 2. Put x = x₁ to get the gradient m at the point. 3. Use y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).
Example. Find the tangent to y = x² + 2x at (1, 3). dy/dx = 2x + 2 = 4 at x = 1. y − 3 = 4(x − 1), so y = 4x − 1.

The normal at a point is the line perpendicular to the tangent there. Its gradient is −1/m. For the same curve at (1, 3): m = 4, so the gradient of the normal is −1/4. y − 3 = −(1/4)(x − 1), so 4y − 12 = −x + 1 and x + 4y = 13.
The tangent to y = x² at P(2, 4). dy/dx = 2x = 4. y − 4 = 4(x − 2), so y = 4x − 4. (The tangent drawn in the earlier figure.)

sections.h: Finding where the gradient has a given value
p: Find the point on y = x² − 4x where the tangent is parallel to the x-axis. dy/dx = 2x − 4 = 0, so x = 2 and y = 4 − 8 = −4. The point is (2, −4).

If f(x) = ax² + bx + c with f′(1) = 8, f′(2) = 14 and f(0) = 5, find a, b and c. f′(x) = 2ax + b, so 2a + b = 8 and 4a + b = 14. Subtract: 2a = 6, so a = 3 and b = 2. f(0) = c = 5. So f(x) = 3x² + 2x + 5.

title: Differentiation II: The Product Rule
summary: How to differentiate a product of two functions, with examples and a check by expanding.

p: If y = uv, where u and v are functions of x, then dy/dx = u (dv/dx) + v (du/dx). In words: first times the derivative of the second plus second times the derivative of the first. Note that the derivative of a product is NOT the product of the derivatives.

y = (2x + 1)(x² − 3). Let u = 2x + 1 and v = x² − 3. Then u′ = 2 and v′ = 2x. dy/dx = u v′ + v u′ = (2x + 1)(2x) + (x² − 3)(2) = 4x² + 2x + 2x² − 6 = 6x² + 2x − 6. Check by expanding: y = 2x³ + x² − 6x − 3, so dy/dx = 6x² + 2x − 6. ✓
y = (x² + 1)(x³ − 2x). u = x² + 1, v = x³ − 2x, u′ = 2x, v′ = 3x² − 2. dy/dx = (x² + 1)(3x² − 2) + (x³ − 2x)(2x) = 3x⁴ + x² − 2 + 2x⁴ − 4x² = 5x⁴ − 3x² − 2.

y = x(2x + 1)³. u = x, v = (2x + 1)³. u′ = 1. For v′ we need the chain rule (next unit): v′ = 3(2x + 1)² × 2 = 6(2x + 1)². dy/dx = (2x + 1)³ + x × 6(2x + 1)² = (2x + 1)²[(2x + 1) + 6x] = (2x + 1)²(8x + 1).
Use the product rule when the expansion would be long. If a product is easy to expand, expanding first and then differentiating each term is also correct.
